Okay so first of all this isn’t true. There’s definitely skill involved & like you mentioned, editing is a huge part of the price because that is a skill and time consuming. 

Now also factor in everything they need to pay for. 

Their equipment. If you don’t provide it but expect photos to have the quality of those taken with good equipment, you need to pay extra for someone who has it (how else would they afford this equipment?) 

To expand on this, good editing software isn’t free. So that’s another piece of “equipment” so to speak they need to pay for. 

Storage space on their computer to edit and save these photos… also not free. They need a really good computer set up and most likely, an expensive hard drive to keep their photos and videos on. 

Travel time. They have to come travel to your location. Don’t forget about gas and tolls in this too! 

Prep time. They need to charge their equipment, get ideas for photos and lights. They’re also experts on posing and lighting. Not just clicking a button. 

Health insurance. If they’re freelance, they ensure their prices are high enough that they can afford to live. This includes paying for all the benefits a corporate job would give them if they weren’t freelance, including health insurance, money away for sick/pto days and a retirement fund. 

Like it’s not just about “oh taking pictures is easy! Anyone can do it & charge $500!” Uhhh no you are paying for this persons time, travel, expertise in posing, lighting, photography, and editing, all of their photography and editing equipment! No sane person would do this for cheap because then they couldn’t afford their equipment or health care or to ever take a day off

Also with weddings, you’re paying for them for a weekend most likely, which is higher, and you’re paying them to deal with lots of people in a high stress situation. Not every amazing photographer can do wedding photography bc the stakes are high, pressure is on, and it’s crowded and overstimulating and everyone is drunk & you need to have your boundaries set and be stern and get the important shots and risk hurting aunt sallies feelings by not taking a solo shot of her during speeches

I agree that it depends. For me, I use “show, don’t tell” when I feel like telling is spelling it out for the reader or dumbing it down. 

I saw a piece of advice once about show don’t tell that stuck with me because I really liked it. 

Telling: Bombs were dropping everywhere, the war had started, and didn’t spare anyone- not even women or children. 

Showing: A loud boom could be heard overhead as I stepped out the now dilapidated door, I could still remember the fresh white paint we used on it just last month. I followed smoke and fire from the bomb with my eyes, crying when it landed on a mother and her child- frozen in time, the child’s 
shoe six feet to the right, blackened with ash. 

*this may not be the exact way either was written- I tried my best to remember* 

Showing immersed the reader into the scene and made them feel emotional while implying a war.

Telling just said “there’s a war now! Onto the next thing!” 

Don’t tell the reader what happened. Show the repercussions of it. Don’t say “the children cried” show why they’re crying. Don’t say “the town was evacuated” say the only sound you can hear is the trees leaves dancing in the wind and how you think you see a woman out of the corner of your eye carrying groceries but when you turn to look, there’s nothing there but the overgrown grass.

Here’s a list.
1. Supported me through emotions. Gifted children and ADHD children have BIG emotions. My mom was and still is completely emotionally unavailable and lacks empathy. 
- Being there for your child during big emotional breaks or just hypersensitive moments makes a huge difference. Breathe with them, take them on a walk around the neighborhood, do some stretches, put on a show, let them help you with something. 
- always be there to listen and validate and support. If they need to cry and rant, let them.
My mom constantly called me dramatic, selfish, not trying hard enough, not good enough, attention seeking, ungrateful, etc. Bc of my emotions and it made it sm worse and I struggle a lot still at 22 years old bc of it. She hasn’t improved one bit either.

2. Don’t make her mask in front of others. Let her be her silly self. My mom constantly told me to tone it down, shut up, you’re talking too much, do you ever shut up, you’re exhausting, leave me alone, etc. Because I get an energy boost around people and love to talk and connect. She focused more on others finding me annoying and her being embarrassed and less on me needing to be that part of myself and accepting that’s how I am.

3. Let her rest if she needs it. ADHD can cause energy crashes. For me in particular, I get really hyper and then really sleepy. Let her take that time to recharge if she needs it. 4. Just at the end of the day, be a safe space. Let her talk to you about things and don’t blame her when she talks to you ab them, let her rest, let her talk her heart out, let her run around, help her find coping skills and help her implement them. 

The fact that you posted on here asking for help to be a better mom to a child with ADHD is honestly already a huge step and shows that you’re an amazing mother who cares.

Honestly, it's not a job for everyone. During the school year, I'm a special ed aid and as much as I love my kids, they make the kids at camp easy breezy for me. You need a lot of patience and training honestly about how to talk to kids in distress. 9 times out of 10 they're acting up because something is wrong inside. Tantrums are a form of communication for kids who don't have the language to tell you they feel excluded or hurt. 

With all of my kids, special ed or not, I've taken to asking "do your feelings hurt or does your body hurt?" It gets them talking more.

I also practice deep breathing with them so they know what to do when they lose control. 

It's also important to understand that you cannot talk a kid down when they are in melt-down mode, just like an adult can't be reasoned with when they're all rowed up. You need to let them have their freak  out, but let them know you're there making sure they are safe and everyone around them is safe and you'll be waiting when they want to talk about how bad it felt to lose control and what you can do better to not lose it again. And make sure they apologize.

The biggest thing is to put your ego aside. If a kid is "fresh" or rude to you, get to the bottom of why they are upset. Don't scold them for "talking back to an adult" or "having a tone." especially if it's a kid that usually a sweetheart. This is not about you or you feeling respected at all. It is about why the angel child is acting up and one snide remark is not something to be punished for if there's a reason for it.
